title: PI-GINOT: Data-free geometry-informed neural operator learning for finite-strain hyperelasticity on parametric DogBone specimens
authors: Aamir Dean, Betim Bahtiri
abstract: Parametric nonlinear solid-mechanics simulations are widely used in virtual testing, optimisation, and uncertainty analysis, but repeated finite-element simulations become costly when geometry changes. This paper presents PI-GINOT, a physics-informed neural operator that predicts finite-strain hyperelastic responses across a four-parameter family of DogBone specimens without using finite-element training data. Each specimen is described by a boundary point cloud, which is encoded into geometry features. A cross-attention decoder then predicts displacement at arbitrary points. Displacement boundary conditions are enforced exactly, while stresses are computed using automatic differentiation and a compressible Neo-Hookean plane-stress model. Training is guided by equilibrium, traction-free and symmetry conditions, deformation stability, and internal force consistency. Abaqus simulations are used only after training for validation. Across eight test geometries, PI-GINOT achieves displacement errors of 2.1%-7.1%, peak von Mises stress errors of 0.9%-13.3%, and section-force errors below 10.3%. Larger errors occur in individual stress components, especially for narrow specimens, mainly because of steep stress gradients near the gauge-to-fillet transition. These results show that PI-GINOT can provide useful geometry-dependent predictions for nonlinear solid mechanics without labelled simulation data, while also revealing where better local stress resolution is still needed.

infographic.key_insight: PI-GINOT learns geometry-conditioned finite-strain hyperelastic responses directly from point-cloud descriptions, enabling data-free prediction across parametric DogBone shapes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It can reduce the need for repeated finite-element simulations in virtual testing, design optimization, and uncertainty studies when specimen geometry changes.
method: Encodes each DogBone boundary point cloud into geometry features.
Uses a cross-attention decoder to predict displacement at arbitrary query points while enforcing boundary conditions exactly.

Computes stresses via automatic differentiation with a compressible Neo-Hookean plane-stress model and trains with physics constraints (equilibrium, traction-free/symmetry, stability, internal-force consistency).
infographic.evidence_signal: On eight unseen geometries, the method reports 2.1%–7.1% displacement error, 0.9%–13.3% peak von Mises stress error, and section-force error below 10.3%, with Abaqus used only for post-training validation.
infographic.watch_item: Local stress components are less accurate near the gauge-to-fillet transition, especially for narrow specimens with steep stress gradients.
infographic.paper_title: PI-GINOT: Data-free geometry-informed neural operator learning for finite-strain hyperelasticity on parametric DogBone specimens

title: A Smooth Explicit Elastoplastic--Damage Update for Graphics Simulation
authors: Yu Ren, Shuangjiu Xiao, Deli Dong
abstract: History-dependent solids require material updates that preserve irreversible deformation and progressive degradation during loading, unloading, and reloading. We present a compact, vectorizable elastoplastic-damage update for explicit graphics simulation, designed for smooth activation and closed-form evaluation rather than exact yield-surface enforcement. A softplus function generates a candidate equivalent plastic strain, a maximum-history projection enforces irreversibility, and a deviatoric plastic-strain tensor retains the residual direction. An exponential scalar degradation variable is driven by the stored history. The active and frozen branches are evaluated analytically from one response energy without a local Newton solve. We evaluate the method using one-dimensional cyclic tension, two-dimensional cantilever bending, controlled three-dimensional platen compression, and a genus-one torus. The results verify residual deformation, monotone internal variables, branchwise energy-gradient agreement, and mesh-resolution sensitivity. An analytical J2 radial-return baseline is compared both as a vectorized kernel and within the same structural solver. The baseline is 1.51--3.08 times faster as a kernel and 1.69 times faster in the structural material update, showing that our contribution is smoothness and implementation simplicity rather than raw speed. A path-direction sweep gives 1.53% normalized equivalent-stress error under proportional loading but 49.39% for a fixed-magnitude 90-degree turn. This quantifies the method's intended restriction to isotropic, proportional or nearly proportional loading; it is not a replacement for general return mapping, anisotropic damage, or phase-field fracture.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a smooth, explicit elastoplastic-damage update that uses closed-form, history-based branches to preserve irreversible plasticity and damage without a local Newton solve.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It is useful for graphics and real-time solid simulation because it favors simple, vectorizable implementation and stable history evolution over exact yield-surface enforcement.
method: Softplus generates a candidate equivalent plastic strain, then a max-history projection enforces irreversibility.
A deviatoric plastic-strain tensor stores residual direction, while an exponential scalar variable drives damage degradation.
Active and frozen branches are evaluated analytically from one response energy, avoiding local nonlinear solves.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors validate the method on 1D cyclic tension, 2D cantilever bending, 3D platen compression, and a torus, and report branchwise energy-gradient agreement, residual deformation, and mesh-resolution sensitivity.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is intended for isotropic, proportional or nearly proportional loading; it degrades sharply under path changes and is not a substitute for general return mapping or anisotropic damage models.
infographic.paper_title: A Smooth Explicit Elastoplastic--Damage Update for Graphics Simulation

title: PIML-OFEM: A New Large-Scale Structural Analysis Method Based on Problem-Independent Machine Learning and Overlapping Finite Element Technique
authors: Yilin Guo, Chang Liu, Zongliang Du, Jin Liu, Jingyu Feng, Xinyang Zhang
abstract: High-resolution analysis and design of large-scale heterogeneous structures require accurate reduced-order models and efficient online computation. Existing multiscale methods must repeatedly construct local basis functions for different material distributions, whereas substructure-based problem-independent machine learning (PIML) methods can be limited by prescribed boundary displacement interpolation. We propose PIML-OFEM, an overlapping finite element method accelerated by problem-independent machine learning. Each substructure retains only its corner-node degrees of freedom. Oversampled numerical basis functions are constructed by solving local elasticity problems on extended domains and restricting the solutions to the target substructure, eliminating prescribed displacement interpolation on its boundary. Independently constructed local bases are blended through a partition-of-unity overlapping formulation to obtain a globally continuous displacement field. A U-Net learns the mapping from local Young's modulus distributions to numerical basis functions, replacing repeated online local solves and allowing the model to be reused across load cases and global boundary conditions. Numerical examples show close agreement with fine-scale finite element results in displacement and elemental strain energy. PIML-OFEM reduces online computational cost relative to direct finite element analysis and improves accuracy over PIML substructure models based on linear boundary interpolation. In topology optimization, the method supports stable high-resolution iterations with small filter radii and preserves fine-scale features, including local patterns resembling rank-2 microstructures. The framework provides an efficient physics-data approach for large-scale heterogeneous structural analysis and high-resolution topology optimization.

infographic.key_insight: PIML-OFEM combines overlapping finite elements with problem-independent machine learning to reuse local basis functions across load cases and boundary conditions for large heterogeneous structures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables faster, high-resolution structural analysis and topology optimization while maintaining accuracy close to fine-scale finite element solutions.
method: Each substructure keeps only corner-node degrees of freedom.
Oversampled local basis functions are computed on extended domains and restricted back to the target substructure.
A U-Net predicts basis functions from local Young's modulus fields, and a partition-of-unity overlap ensures global continuity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports close agreement with fine-scale FEM for displacement and elemental strain energy, with lower online cost than direct FEM and better accuracy than PIML substructure models using linear boundary interpolation.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on learning reliable basis mappings from representative material distributions, so performance may degrade for unseen heterogeneity or poorly covered training sets.
infographic.paper_title: PIML-OFEM: A New Large-Scale Structural Analysis Method Based on Problem-Independent Machine Learning and Overlapping Finite Element Technique

title: Uncertainty-quantified $J$-integral computation for quasicontinuum and finite element methods
authors: Sai Harshith Badi, Stephen M. Whalen, Ronald E. Miller, Ellad B. Tadmor
abstract: The $J$-integral is a fundamental concept in fracture mechanics, quantifying the energy release rate that drives crack propagation. While extensively implemented in finite element (FE) codes and adapted for atomistic calculations, its application within multiscale frameworks bridging atomistic and continuum formulations remains unexplored. This work presents a rigorous implementation and validation of the $J$-integral within the three-dimensional quasicontinuum (QC3D) method, computed under plane strain assumptions, using continuum fields (stress, strain energy density) derived from the interatomic potential via the Cauchy-Born rule. The implementation is validated against linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) theory and the virtual crack extension (VCE) method across three regimes: (1) small-strain linear elasticity, with a prescribed anisotropic $K$-field displacement applied throughout; (2) the same field evaluated through the nonlinear Cauchy-Born constitutive relation, without atomic relaxation; and (3) the same relation with atomic relaxation enabled, allowing the crack-tip region to equilibrate. Excellent agreement is shown throughout. We further introduce a Markov chain Monte Carlo framework to statistically quantify the uncertainty of $J$-integral results for a given mesh and integration domain, applicable to conventional FE methods as well. Predictive capability is demonstrated via a QC3D simulation of a three-point bending test of silicon, where the computed critical energy release rate agrees closely with the Griffith criterion. This work establishes a reliable framework for evaluating crack driving forces in multiscale fracture simulations with quantified uncertainty, enabling large-scale fracture simulations while resolving atomistic mechanisms at the crack tip.

infographic.key_insight: The paper extends the J-integral to 3D quasicontinuum fracture simulations and adds uncertainty quantification so crack-driving force estimates can be validated and trusted in multiscale settings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives fracture engineers a practical way to compute energy release rates in atomistic-continuum models, supporting large-scale crack simulations while still resolving tip-scale physics.
method: Implemented the J-integral in QC3D under plane strain using Cauchy-Born-derived stress and strain energy density fields.
Validated results against LEFM and the virtual crack extension method across elastic, nonlinear, and atomically relaxed regimes.
Added a Markov chain Monte Carlo procedure to quantify uncertainty from mesh and integration-domain choices.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports excellent agreement with LEFM/VCE in three regimes and close agreement between predicted and Griffith critical energy release rates in a silicon three-point bending simulation.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on mesh quality, integration-domain selection, and plane-strain/Cauchy-Born assumptions, so careful setup is needed for robust results.
infographic.paper_title: Uncertainty-quantified $J$-integral computation for quasicontinuum and finite element methods

title: Interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANN and fPANN) for uncertainty quantification and propagation in constitutive modeling
authors: Somesh Pratap Singh, Govinda Anantha Padmanabha, Jingye Tan, Steven Yang, Reese E. Jones, D. Thomas Seidl
abstract: Constitutive modeling under uncertainty remains a central challenge for reliable mechanics simulations, particularly when the available stress-deformation data are sparse, noisy, or heterogeneous. We propose interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANNs and fPANNs) for uncertainty-aware hyperelastic constitutive modeling. iPANNs learn sparse lower, mean, and upper free energy density branches whose stresses, obtained by automatic differentiation, ultimately enclose noisy stress observations. In contrast to this deterministic interval description, fPANNs embed the learned iPANN branches into a fuzzy-set representation through alpha-cut interpolation, yielding a nested family of admissible responses. iPANNs and fPANNs encode mechanistic constraints - preserving objectivity, consistency and promoting polyconvexity - and smoothed L0 regularization promotes interpretable energy representations. The bound models are trained through a two-stage transfer-learning procedure in which a sparse mean constitutive response is learned first and then fine-tuned into lower and upper energy branches. We evaluate the framework on synthetic isotropic hyperelastic data with heteroscedastic noise, varying random realizations, shifted noise means, and varying noise magnitudes. The results show that the learned bounds enclose noisy stress observations while generalizing to the test set. Further, we examine the propagation of uncertainty through the mean, upper and lower bound predictions of the learned iPANN models in a finite element setting. The proposed framework provides a compact, physics-consistent route for distribution-free aleatoric uncertainty quantification in hyperelastic constitutive modeling, and propagation in downstream finite element simulations.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks that learn physically constrained lower/mean/upper free-energy branches to quantify and propagate constitutive uncertainty.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives mechanics engineers a distribution-free way to build hyperelastic models that remain interpretable, data-efficient, and usable in finite element simulations under noisy or sparse stress data.
method: Two-stage transfer learning: fit a sparse mean energy model first, then fine-tune lower and upper branches.
Use automatic differentiation to convert learned free-energy densities into stress predictions.
Embed interval branches into a fuzzy-set representation via alpha-cut interpolation and enforce mechanistic constraints with smoothed L0 regularization.
infographic.evidence_signal: On synthetic isotropic hyperelastic data with heteroscedastic noise, shifted noise means, and varying noise magnitudes, the learned bounds enclosed noisy stress observations and generalized to the test set.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on careful training of the bound branches and constraint/regularization settings, so robustness on real experimental datasets with stronger heterogeneity still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Interval and fuzzy physics-augmented neural networks (iPANN and fPANN) for uncertainty quantification and propagation in constitutive modeling

title: $\partial^2 ( \mathrm{TO} ) $: A Dual Topological Derivative-Based Enriched Topology Optimization for Fracture Mitigation in 3-D Brittle Solids
authors: Majd Kosta, Shangru Liu, Alejandro M. Aragón
abstract: We propose a fracture-mitigation topology optimization framework for 3-D brittle solids. The topology is described by a level set function parameterized by radial basis functions, and the structural response is computed using an interface-enriched finite element formulation. Dual topological derivatives serve two purposes. First, they are used to nucleate holes within the solid during the optimization process. Second, they are used to evaluate energy release rates (ERRs) along the entire boundary, requiring only the stress field from a single enriched finite element analysis of the uncracked geometry. For this purpose, penny-shaped cracks are assumed to nucleate using the maximum hoop stress criterion, at the locations of enriched nodes introduced along the boundary for accurate finite element analysis. Because ERR estimates depend sensitively on stress accuracy, we compute a nodal stress field using a non-local stress-recovery procedure. The topology optimization objective aggregates the boundary ERRs using a $p$-mean function. Three-dimensional numerical examples, including the commonly studied L-bracket benchmark problem, demonstrate the capability of the proposed framework.

infographic.key_insight: A dual topological-derivative framework uses one enriched 3-D stress analysis to both remove material and predict crack-driving energy release rates, enabling fracture-aware topology optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This lets engineers design brittle structures that are not only lightweight but also less prone to crack initiation, with direct relevance to high-stakes 3-D components.
method: Level set topology is parameterized with radial basis functions and updated via optimization.
An interface-enriched finite element method computes stresses on the uncracked geometry.
Dual topological derivatives are used to nucleate holes and estimate boundary energy release rates; a p-mean aggregates the crack-risk measure.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 3-D numerical examples, including the L-bracket benchmark, to demonstrate the framework’s fracture-mitigation capability.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends sensitively on stress accuracy and on assumptions such as penny-shaped crack nucleation and maximum hoop stress criterion, so robust implementation is critical.
infographic.paper_title: $\partial^2 ( \mathrm{TO} ) $: A Dual Topological Derivative-Based Enriched Topology Optimization for Fracture Mitigation in 3-D Brittle Solids

title: Thermo-Structural Topology Optimization Considering Nonlinear Creep
authors: Stefan Knapik, Aaditya Chandrasekhar, Deepak Sharma, Jian Cao, Changjie Sun, Wei Chen
abstract: Creep is a primary life-limiting mechanism for metallic components operating at high temperature, producing permanent deformation under sustained loads even when stresses remain below yield. The design of structures to minimize this deformation is critical to extending the service life of components. Incorporating creep into topology optimization (TO) remains open because the response is nonlinear, history-dependent, and thermomechanically coupled, and prior work often relies on linear viscoelastic models, which do not capture the behavior of metals at high temperatures. To bridge this gap, we introduce a differentiable thermo-structural TO framework. The approach considers creep deformation using the Norton model and leverages JAX's automatic differentiation to perform adjoint sensitivity analysis, enabling efficient gradient-based optimization. The transient material response is solved via a backward Euler scheme over a prescribed service life. Our objective is to minimize creep deformation subject to a volume constraint. We first demonstrate the framework on canonical two-dimensional benchmarks, showing that the proposed formulation significantly reduces permanent deformation compared to designs optimized solely for elastic stiffness. We then pose, as a challenge problem, the compositional design of a three-dimensional graded material turbine blade in which the local mixture of two candidate alloys is optimized. This challenge problem exercises the full capability of the framework, including transient nonlinear creep, coupled thermal loading, three-dimensional geometry, and gradient-based multi-material design, highlighting the need for creep-aware design in high-temperature applications.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that topology optimization can be extended to high-temperature components by directly optimizing against nonlinear creep deformation instead of only elastic stiffness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables safer, longer-life designs for metallic parts such as turbine blades operating under sustained thermal and mechanical loads.
method: Uses a differentiable thermo-structural topology optimization framework with the Norton creep model.
Solves transient creep response with backward Euler over the service life and uses JAX automatic differentiation for adjoint sensitivities.
Supports gradient-based optimization for 2D benchmarks and a 3D graded-material turbine blade design challenge.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports benchmark studies showing substantially lower permanent deformation than elastic-stiffness-only designs, plus a 3D turbine blade challenge demonstrating the framework under coupled thermal, nonlinear, and multi-material conditions.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on accurate creep constitutive parameters and a differentiable transient solver, so results may be sensitive to material-model calibration and computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: Thermo-Structural Topology Optimization Considering Nonlinear Creep

title: A Least Squares Weak Galerkin Framework for Linear Elasticity on Polytopal Meshes
authors: Chunmei Wang, Shangyou Zhang
abstract: This paper develops and analyzes a least-squares weak Galerkin (LS-WG) finite element method for linear elasticity. By employing weak differential operators, specifically the weak gradient, weak strain tensor, and weak divergence, defined on weak finite element spaces, the proposed framework facilitates the treatment of complex boundary conditions and internal interfaces while avoiding the restrictive discrete inf-sup condition. The resulting formulation is symmetric and positive definite and exhibits robust numerical performance in the nearly incompressible regime. In addition, the proposed method offers exceptional geometric flexibility, allowing implementation on general polytopal (polygonal and polyhedral) meshes. We establish the uniqueness of the numerical solution and derive optimal-order error estimates with respect to a tailored discrete energy norm. Extensive numerical experiments confirm the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate the method's stability, efficiency, and locking-free performance for nearly incompressible materials.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a least-squares weak Galerkin finite element framework that solves linear elasticity on general polytopal meshes with a symmetric positive definite formulation and no discrete inf-sup constraint.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes the method attractive for structural mechanics problems with complex geometry, irregular meshes, and nearly incompressible materials where locking and boundary-condition handling are challenging.
method: Uses weak differential operators: weak gradient, weak strain tensor, and weak divergence.
Formulates elasticity as a least-squares weak Galerkin method on weak finite element spaces.
Designed for polygonal/polyhedral meshes and robust treatment of boundary conditions and interfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports optimal-order error estimates and extensive numerical experiments showing stability, efficiency, and locking-free performance in the nearly incompressible regime.
infographic.watch_item: Practical deployment may require careful construction of weak spaces and local operators to preserve stability and accuracy on highly irregular polytopal meshes.
infographic.paper_title: A Least Squares Weak Galerkin Framework for Linear Elasticity on Polytopal Meshes

title: No Free Lunch in Flow Surrogates under Time-Varying Boundary Conditions: A Two-Regime Study
authors: Georg Winkler, Martin Stoll
abstract: A flow surrogate validated on a simple regime is often taken as evidence that the approach will carry to a richer one. We test this assumption on two transient flows under time-varying boundary conditions emulating the process startup: the three-dimensional slurry film in chemical-mechanical planarisation (CMP), a core semiconductor-manufacturing process, and the two-dimensional Karman vortex street (KVS) behind a cylinder. Eight surrogate models are compared on one shared evaluation pipeline, differing in whether they learn the full field or a latent representation, and whether they predict trajectories in one shot or step by step. No single architecture wins both regimes. On the film, a one-shot full-field model reconstructs the process-relevant cumulative wall shear stress to 3.2% relative error. On the wake, a latent autoregressive DeepONet retains 96% of the shedding power that direct and one-shot models damp to almost zero. The deciding axis is the treatment of time. The self-sustained wake requires the phase memory that autoregressive feedback provides, while the boundary-driven film rewards a direct map. Pointwise RMSE picks the wrong model in both regimes, so the evaluation scores five physical questions instead, the field, its structure, invented motion, amplitude, and timing. The trained surrogates answer queries $10^3$ to $10^4$ times faster than the finite-element solver, but the offline cost of the training simulations means they pay off from the first query beyond the training set for CMP and the third for the KVS. The choice of surrogate should follow the dynamical character of the target flow, and its validation should use failure-mode-resolved metrics, since neither the winning architecture nor its validation transfers.

infographic.key_insight: There is no universally best flow surrogate: the right architecture depends on whether the dynamics are boundary-driven or self-sustained, with time handling being the deciding factor.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For process and fluid simulations, surrogate selection should match the physics and validation should use failure-mode-specific metrics rather than pointwise RMSE alone.
method: Compared 8 surrogate architectures across two transient flow regimes: CMP slurry film and cylinder wake (Karman vortex street).
Varied representation style (full-field vs latent) and rollout style (one-shot vs autoregressive/stepwise).
Evaluated models with five physical criteria: field accuracy, structure, invented motion, amplitude, and timing.
infographic.evidence_signal: A one-shot full-field model reached 3.2% relative error on cumulative wall shear stress in CMP, while an autoregressive latent DeepONet preserved 96% of wake shedding power that other models nearly eliminated.
infographic.watch_item: Offline training cost matters: the surrogate only pays off after enough queries, so deployment value depends on the number of post-training evaluations and the regime-specific setup.
infographic.paper_title: No Free Lunch in Flow Surrogates under Time-Varying Boundary Conditions: A Two-Regime Study

title: Synaptic clustering emerges from learning and supports covariance discrimination
authors: Ilenna Simone Jones, Maceo Richards, Houman Safaai, Elom Amematsro, Bernardo Sabatini
abstract: Functional synapse clusters (FSCs) are synapses with correlated presynaptic activity that are colocalized on the same neuronal dendritic branch. FSCs have been observed after learning in cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons. However, previous efforts to ablate FSCs by pharmacologically blocking dendritic nonlinearities to establish causal necessity may have confounded effects. Therefore, whether FSCs are causally necessary for computation is unknown. Here, we attempt to isolate FSCs from this potential confounder in silico. We train Dendrinet, an artificial neural network architecture with hierarchical dendritic segments and sparse conductance-based synapses, on a Permuted-Covariance Classification (PCC) task. This task cannot be solved by single-layer linear-nonlinear artificial neural networks. We find that neurons with dendrites can be trained to solve the task and develop excitatory and inhibitory FSCs if both dendritic nonlinearities and synaptic structural plasticity are active. Turning off dendritic nonlinearities reduces excitatory FSCs, which replicates experimental findings, and reduces performance while unexpectedly increasing inhibitory FSCs. Furthermore, shuffling learned synaptic connectivity while keeping the nonlinearities fixed reduces performance. This shows sensitivity to learned connectivity, but the shuffle does not change only FSCs. Shuffling inhibitory synapse properties reduces performance more than the corresponding excitatory shuffle, showing higher sensitivity to inhibitory organization. This work suggests that dendritic compartmentalization and learned synaptic organization can support computation of covariance structure.

infographic.key_insight: Learning can organize synapses into dendritic clusters that improve a neuron’s ability to discriminate covariance structure, but only when dendritic nonlinearities and synaptic structural plasticity both remain active.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result suggests that distributed, compartmentalized connectivity may be a design principle for neuro-inspired hardware and models that need to encode higher-order correlations beyond linear separability.
method: Built Dendrinet, a neural network with hierarchical dendritic segments and sparse conductance-based synapses.
Trained the model on a Permuted-Covariance Classification task that single-layer linear-nonlinear networks cannot solve.
Tested causal roles by turning off dendritic nonlinearities and shuffling learned excitatory/inhibitory synaptic organization.
infographic.evidence_signal: In silico evaluation showed the dendritic model could solve the task and form excitatory and inhibitory synaptic clusters, while disabling nonlinearities or shuffling learned connectivity reduced performance.
infographic.watch_item: The results are model-based and shuffling interventions may alter more than just functional synaptic clustering, so causal interpretations should be made cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Synaptic clustering emerges from learning and supports covariance discrimination

title: From Execution to Capability: Scientific Experience Consolidation via Procedural Knowledge Synthesis
authors: Liwei Dong, Jiahao Zhao, Nan Xu
abstract: Large language models increasingly solve scientific-computing tasks, but executable feedback from one problem rarely becomes durable capability on subsequent problems. We study scientific-computing experience consolidation: converting verified runtime experience into transferable procedural knowledge and persistent model improvement. This setting presents two challenges: trajectory-derived artifacts may encode source-specific repairs rather than cross-task computational mechanisms; and a weaker target model may be unable to operationalize an otherwise valid abstract procedure - an abstraction-execution gap. We introduce SciConsolidate, which contrasts verified successes and failures to induce cross-task procedures, selects them through a development-validation gate, and uses failure-informed, answer-free query synthesis to expand the consolidation data without requiring pre-existing reference answers. Because the target model may not directly execute these abstractions, a stronger model concretizes them into executable code supervision for standard, procedure-free SFT; a matched no-procedure teacher branch isolates the value of procedural guidance. On SciCode, runtime procedure injection improves Qwen3.6-27B by +3.85/+6.26 sub-step/main-problem points, but yields almost no aggregate main-problem gain for Qwen3.5-9B, providing operational evidence of the abstraction-execution gap. After procedure-guided concretization, the 9B student improves under procedure-free deployment by +3.89/+6.25 points over the no-procedure SFT control and by +5.62/+11.25 over the original 9B model. These results establish an experience-to-capability pathway for scientific computing and provide a practical starting point for scaling self-improving scientific assistance.

infographic.key_insight: Verified runtime experiences can be consolidated into reusable procedural knowledge, but smaller models may need that knowledge concretized before it improves performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For scientific computing and fracture/damage workflows, the method suggests a path from one-off solver feedback to durable assistant behavior that can generalize across tasks.
method: Contrast verified successes and failures to extract cross-task procedures.
Use a development-validation gate plus failure-informed, answer-free query synthesis to grow consolidation data.
Have a stronger teacher concretize procedures into executable code for procedure-free SFT, with a no-procedure control for comparison.
infographic.evidence_signal: On SciCode, procedure injection improved Qwen3.6-27B by +3.85/+6.26 sub-step/main-problem points, while the 9B student only improved after procedure-guided concretization (+3.89/+6.25 over control; +5.62/+11.25 over baseline).
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on a stronger model to bridge the abstraction-execution gap, so gains may not transfer if the student cannot reliably operationalize abstract procedures.
infographic.paper_title: From Execution to Capability: Scientific Experience Consolidation via Procedural Knowledge Synthesis

title: A Mixed Discrete Cosserat Rod Formulation
authors: Tianxiang Dai, Marco Herrmann, Jonas Breuling, Remco I. Leine, Simon R. Eugster
abstract: In this communication we propose a discrete Cosserat rod formulation in which a slender elastic rod is represented as a chain of rigid bodies (nodes) coupled by compliant elastic forces and moments acting between adjacent node pairs. Discrete dilatation, shear, torsion and curvature strain measures are evaluated from the relative kinematics of each node pair, while the constitutive behavior is expressed in compliance form through independent stress degrees of freedom. We show that the resulting model arises rigorously from a mixed Petrov--Galerkin Cosserat rod finite element formulation (FEM) at linear kinematic interpolation order when the internal virtual work is integrated by the midpoint rule and the external and inertial contributions by the trapezoidal rule. The proposed formulation inherits the robustness and the absence of locking from the underlying mixed FEM while simultaneously exposing a two-node coupling structure that mirrors discrete rod models from the computer graphics community. This is in sharp contrast to the dense coupling of strain-parameterized reduced-order models often used in soft robotic applications. Three numerical examples involving piecewise-varying cross sections, tendon-driven actuation under different spatial discretizations, and coupled longitudinal-torsional dynamics confirm the accuracy, robustness, and convergence behavior of the presented approach.

infographic.key_insight: A Cosserat rod can be reformulated as a chain of rigid nodes with pairwise compliant forces/moments, while retaining the rigor and anti-locking benefits of a mixed finite element derivation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives a robust, two-node-coupled rod model suitable for soft robotics and slender-structure dynamics, with simpler discrete mechanics than dense reduced-order strain models.
method: Mixed Petrov–Galerkin Cosserat rod FEM with linear kinematic interpolation
Internal virtual work integrated by midpoint rule; external and inertial terms by trapezoidal rule
Independent stress DOFs in compliance form for dilatation, shear, torsion, and curvature
infographic.evidence_signal: Three numerical examples—varying cross sections, tendon-driven actuation, and coupled longitudinal-torsional dynamics—show accuracy, robustness, and convergence.
infographic.watch_item: The formulation’s accuracy depends on correct discrete integration and pairwise coupling setup, so implementation details may be critical for stability and consistency.
infographic.paper_title: A Mixed Discrete Cosserat Rod Formulation

title: PG-KINN: A Physics-Informed Petrov-Galerkin Kolmogorov-Arnold Network for Solving Forward and Inverse PDEs
authors: Amirhossein Sadr, Nima Soltani, Vahideh Moghtadaiee, Aida Pakniyat, Dara Rahmati, Saeid Gorgin
abstract: Physics-informed learning of partial differential equations (PDEs) has been dominated by multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), whose spectral bias and dense parameterization limit both accuracy and interpretability. Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KANs) mitigate these limitations because their learnable spline activations are structurally aligned with the piecewise-polynomial bases of classical discretizations. However, the way a PDE is cast into a loss functional is as decisive as the choice of approximator: strong-form residual minimization requires high-order derivatives and heavily weighted losses, the energy (Bubnov-Galerkin) form is restricted to self-adjoint operators and, as we show, collapses to a trivial solution for parameter-identification problems, and boundary integral forms require a known fundamental solution. We propose PG-KINN, a physics-informed KAN built on a Petrov-Galerkin formulation in which the trial space is a KAN and the test space is an independent, compactly supported, piecewise-polynomial space evaluated with Gauss-Legendre quadrature. Integration by parts lowers the differentiation order while retaining applicability to general non-self-adjoint, nonlinear, and inverse problems; the localized test functions turn the global residual into a set of element-wise weak residuals with favorable conditioning. On a suite of benchmarks spanning crack singularities, stress concentration, Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, inverse parameter identification in heterogeneous media, and complex geometries, PG-KINN consistently outperforms legacy MLP baselines and state-of-the-art KAN-based strong/energy/inverse formulations (PIKAN). These results position the Petrov-Galerkin coupling of KAN trial spaces and polynomial test spaces as a robust and accurate route for AI-based computational mechanics.

infographic.key_insight: PG-KINN couples a KAN trial network with an independent Petrov-Galerkin test space to make physics-informed PDE learning more accurate, stable, and broadly applicable than strong-form or energy-form approaches.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is useful for solid mechanics and constitutive modeling because it handles nonlinear, non-self-adjoint, and inverse PDEs while reducing derivative order and improving conditioning.
method: Use a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network as the trial function approximator.
Use compactly supported piecewise-polynomial test functions with Gauss-Legendre quadrature.
Form a weak Petrov-Galerkin residual via integration by parts for forward and inverse PDEs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent gains over MLP baselines and prior KAN-based strong/energy/inverse methods across benchmarks including crack singularities, stress concentration, Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, inverse identification, and complex geometries.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on careful implementation of the weak form, quadrature, and localized test-space design, and the abstract does not report detailed computational cost or robustness limits.
infographic.paper_title: PG-KINN: A Physics-Informed Petrov-Galerkin Kolmogorov-Arnold Network for Solving Forward and Inverse PDEs

title: A Hyper-Reduced Neural Network-Augmented Semi-smooth Newton Method for Nonlinear Parametric Variational Inequalities
authors: Sofiane Ezzehi, Virginie Ehrlacher, Guillaume Enchéry, Thibault Faney
abstract: We propose a model order reduction framework for nonlinear parametrized variational inequalities arising in computational mechanics. The high-dimensional model is written in mixed primal-dual form with projection-based complementarity conditions, leading to nonlinear nonsmooth algebraic systems solved by a semi-smooth Newton method in primal-dual form. On this basis, reduced models are constructed by proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) of both primal and dual solution snapshots, and the resulting reduced systems are solved by semi-smooth Newton iterations in the reduced space. To address cases where low-dimensional linear spaces provide limited approximation efficiency, we introduce a neural-network-augmented reduced model. Two feedforward networks learn corrections in the truncated POD coordinates of the primal and dual variables, defining a nonlinear manifold approximation that is embedded directly in the semi-smooth Newton iterations. The online cost associated with high-dimensional residual evaluations is reduced through hyper-reduction, using a sparse cubature approach based on greedy nonnegative least squares. Particular attention is paid to the interaction between hyper-reduction and the learned nonlinear manifold. The proposed methodology is assessed on two nonlinear variational inequalities with distinct sources of nonlinearity: a two-dimensional obstacle problem with a cubic nonlinearity in the state equation, and a three-dimensional frictional contact problem in which the Coulomb law induces a nonlinear projection in the constraint equation. Numerical results compare the high-dimensional model, the linear reduced model, the neural-network-augmented reduced model, and their hyper-reduced variants, demonstrating accurate approximations with substantial reductions in online computational cost.

infographic.key_insight: A semi-smooth Newton reduced-order framework, augmented with neural corrections and hyper-reduction, can efficiently solve nonlinear parametric variational inequalities in solid mechanics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster surrogate simulation of contact and obstacle-type mechanics problems while preserving the primal-dual structure needed for accurate constraint handling.
method: Build POD reduced bases for both primal and dual solution snapshots.
Add two feedforward networks to correct truncated POD coordinates and form a nonlinear manifold.
Use sparse-cubature hyper-reduction with greedy nonnegative least squares to cut online residual costs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical tests on a 2D obstacle problem and a 3D frictional contact problem, comparing full-order, linear reduced, neural-augmented, and hyper-reduced variants with substantial online cost reductions.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality of snapshot training and on how well hyper-reduction preserves the nonlinear complementarity structure during Newton iterations.
infographic.paper_title: A Hyper-Reduced Neural Network-Augmented Semi-smooth Newton Method for Nonlinear Parametric Variational Inequalities

title: Goal-Oriented Error Estimation for Least-Squares Finite Element Methods via Physically Meaningful Adjoint PDEs
authors: Yueyao Wu, Shun Zhang
abstract: We develop a goal-oriented error-estimation framework for first-order system least-squares (FOSLS) finite element methods based on the physical PDE adjoint rather than the adjoint induced by the least-squares formulation. Identified explicitly from the differential operator, its mixed boundary conditions, and the output, the physical adjoint admits its own first-order flux system and hence a native, built-in least-squares estimator, which the least-squares-induced adjoint does not. Our error identities rest on a primal-dual corrected functional: they follow from the continuous primal and adjoint equations alone, hold for arbitrary conforming approximations, and require no Galerkin orthogonality. For outputs containing a weighted Dirichlet-boundary flux, whose weight becomes the essential datum of the adjoint, we construct two corrected approximations, one from the potentials and one also using the fluxes, and prove product-type error estimates in the primal and adjoint errors. The least-squares functionals then yield computable a posteriori bounds and a balanced marking indicator whose element sum equals the product of the two estimators exactly. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence and the effectiveness of the marking.

infographic.key_insight: The paper replaces the usual least-squares-induced adjoint with the physically defined PDE adjoint, enabling goal-oriented error estimates that remain valid for arbitrary conforming approximations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives FEM practitioners a more faithful and computable way to estimate and drive refinement for specific outputs, especially when boundary flux terms matter.
method: Derive the adjoint directly from the differential operator, mixed boundary conditions, and output functional.
Build a first-order flux system for the physical adjoint so it also admits a native least-squares estimator.
Use primal-dual corrected functionals to obtain error identities and computable a posteriori bounds without Galerkin orthogonality.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments in the abstract confirm the predicted convergence and show the balanced marking strategy is effective.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on correctly identifying the physical adjoint and its essential boundary data, which may be delicate for complex outputs or boundary conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Goal-Oriented Error Estimation for Least-Squares Finite Element Methods via Physically Meaningful Adjoint PDEs

title: AlgMortar: a fully algebraic multiscale mortar preconditioner
authors: Luan F. Santos, Fabricio S. Sousa, Roberto F. Ausas, Rafael T. Guiraldello, Felipe Pereira
abstract: The solution of large-scale symmetric positive definite linear systems arising from discretizations of second-order elliptic equations is challenging, especially in applications with highly heterogeneous coefficients, such as flow in porous media, which can lead to severely ill-conditioned systems. In this context, multiscale methods have recently been used to accelerate Krylov subspace methods, owing to their favorable parallel scalability. In this work, we present AlgMortar, a fully algebraic realization of the Multiscale Mortar Mixed Finite Element Method (MMMFEM). The method uses only information extracted from the fine-grid system matrix, which facilitates its implementation in existing solvers. AlgMortar uses graph partitioning to define a domain decomposition directly from the matrix graph. On each subdomain, it builds local linear systems that mimic Dirichlet problems, and couples the resulting local solutions through an algebraic interface condition that recovers the weak flux-continuity mechanism of MMMFEM. We prove that the method is well posed when the fine-grid matrix is symmetric positive definite and has nonpositive off-diagonal entries, a structure commonly arising from discretizations of elliptic problems. Numerical experiments on fine-grid linear systems arising from finite-volume discretizations of Darcy flow problems show that, when used as a preconditioner for the conjugate gradient method, the proposed approach exhibits good scalability and is competitive with state-of-the-art algebraic multigrid methods for challenging heterogeneous, high-contrast test cases, including highly irregular corner-point grids.

infographic.key_insight: AlgMortar turns a multiscale mortar preconditioner into a fully algebraic, matrix-only method that can efficiently accelerate Krylov solvers for heterogeneous elliptic systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a practical preconditioning strategy for large, ill-conditioned flow and porous-media simulations where standard solvers struggle with high-contrast coefficients.
method: Partition the matrix graph into subdomains using graph partitioning.
Solve local Dirichlet-like problems on each subdomain using only fine-grid matrix information.
Couple subdomain solutions with an algebraic interface condition that enforces weak flux continuity.
infographic.evidence_signal: In Darcy-flow finite-volume tests, AlgMortar used as a CG preconditioner showed good scalability and competitive performance versus state-of-the-art algebraic multigrid, including difficult high-contrast and irregular corner-point grids.
infographic.watch_item: The method’s well-posedness is proved under SPD matrices with nonpositive off-diagonal entries, so performance and guarantees may be more limited outside this matrix class.
infographic.paper_title: AlgMortar: a fully algebraic multiscale mortar preconditioner

title: High-order finite element method for perfect conductivity and linear elasticity with nearly touching inclusions
authors: Buyang Li, Haigang Li, Yonglin Li, Peihao Zhang
abstract: In perfect conductivity and linear elasticity problems, the electric field and stress always become highly concentrated within narrow regions between adjacent perfect (rigid) inclusions, and blow up as the distance between inclusions approaches zero. The design of high-order numerical methods with rigorous error analysis for such concentration problems remains open. In this paper, we present the first high-order finite element method for solving these problems. Our approach is based on asymptotic estimates of high-order derivatives of solutions, employing a graded mesh and auxiliary basis functions specifically designed from these derivative estimates. We prove that the proposed method converges with an $H^1$-error bound of $O(h^p)$ and the error bound is independent of the distance (possibly approaching zero) between inclusions, where $h$ is the mesh size and $p$ is the degree of finite elements. Numerical examples in both two and three dimensions are presented to demonstrate the convergence rates of the numerical solutions. In particular, the blow-up behaviors of the gradients of solutions are demonstrated when the inclusions approach each other.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces the first high-order finite element method that remains accurate for perfect conductivity and linear elasticity problems with nearly touching inclusions, even as gradients blow up.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables reliable simulation of stress and electric-field concentration in composite materials and microstructures where small gaps between rigid/perfect inclusions control failure or performance.
method: Derive asymptotic estimates for high-order solution derivatives near nearly touching inclusions.
Use a graded mesh to resolve narrow gap regions efficiently.
Construct auxiliary basis functions from the derivative estimates to support high-order FEM accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 2D and 3D numerical examples showing the expected convergence rates and demonstrating gradient blow-up as the inclusion gap shrinks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and implementation may be sensitive to mesh grading and auxiliary basis construction, especially in complex 3D geometries.
infographic.paper_title: High-order finite element method for perfect conductivity and linear elasticity with nearly touching inclusions

title: Stability and error analysis of IMEX-BDFk finite element schemes for the incompressible Navier-Stokes system
authors: Qianqian Ding, Yifan Luo, Shipeng Mao
abstract: In this paper, we propose and analyze a class of high-order numerical schemes within a fully discrete finite element framework for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with no-slip boundary conditions. The temporal discretization employs a kth-order (k=1,...,6) implicit-explicit backward difference formula (IMEX-BDFk), in which the nonlinear convection term is treated explicitly and the linear Stokes part implicitly, whereas the spatial discretization utilizes Taylor-Hood finite elements. We establish the stability and uniform boundedness of the numerical solution. We further establish optimal order error estimates in both space and time without any CFL-type condition, in the sense that the time step is independent of the spatial mesh size. In three dimensions, these include L2- and H1-norm error estimates for the velocity and L2-norm error estimates for the pressure, with temporal convergence rates up to sixth order for all variables. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the scheme and to confirm the theoretical convergence rates.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that high-order IMEX-BDFk finite element schemes can stably and accurately solve incompressible Navier-Stokes flow without requiring a CFL-type time-step restriction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical, high-order time integration strategy for CFD and fluid-structure-related simulations where stability, accuracy, and mesh-independent time stepping are important.
method: IMEX-BDFk time stepping for k=1 to 6
Explicit treatment of nonlinear convection; implicit treatment of the linear Stokes operator
Taylor-Hood finite elements for spatial discretization
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors prove stability, uniform boundedness, and optimal error estimates, and report numerical experiments that confirm the predicted convergence rates up to sixth order.
infographic.watch_item: The scheme’s efficiency and robustness depend on careful implementation of high-order IMEX-BDF steps and compatible Taylor-Hood discretization, especially in 3D problems.
infographic.paper_title: Stability and error analysis of IMEX-BDFk finite element schemes for the incompressible Navier-Stokes system

title: Scaling Limits of Multichannel Spectral Routers for Snapshot Imaging
authors: Junseo Han, Seunghyun Lee, Donghyun Kim, Haejun Chung
abstract: Inverse-designed spectral routers can enable compact snapshot spectral imaging by directing different wavelengths to designated detector sub-pixels without mechanical scanning or absorptive filters. Here, we examine how routing performance varies as the number of spectral channels increases while the visible bandwidth remains fixed. A delay-bandwidth analysis relates channel count, worst-channel efficiency, and device thickness, explaining the growing optical capacity required to generate many spatially distinct spectral outputs. We then use adjoint-based topology optimization and three-dimensional finite-difference time-domain simulations to design TiO2/SiO2 routers with 9, 16, 25, and 36 channels under matched material, bandwidth, and thickness conditions. The average routing efficiency increases with sub-pixel size and approaches a plateau, while the maximum near-plateau efficiency decreases monotonically from 97.0% for 9 channels to 82.3% for 36 channels. At a fixed channel count, compressing the wavelength spacing to 8 nm or rearranging the wavelength-to-sub-pixel assignment changes the efficiency by less than one percentage point. These results indicate that the observed efficiency penalty is governed mainly by the number of wavelength-dependent routing constraints rather than by wavelength spacing or local wavelength arrangement. The findings quantify the trade-off between spectral sampling and optical throughput in compact snapshot spectral imagers.

infographic.key_insight: As the number of spectral channels grows at fixed bandwidth and thickness, inverse-designed spectral routers face a fundamental throughput penalty: more routing constraints demand more optical capacity, lowering best-case efficiency.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This quantifies the design trade-off for compact snapshot spectral imagers, helping engineers balance spectral resolution against detector throughput and device miniaturization.
method: Used delay-bandwidth analysis to relate channel count, efficiency, and thickness.
Designed TiO2/SiO2 spectral routers with adjoint-based topology optimization.
Verified performance with 3D finite-difference time-domain simulations for 9, 16, 25, and 36 channels.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across matched conditions, the maximum near-plateau routing efficiency decreased from 97.0% at 9 channels to 82.3% at 36 channels, while changing wavelength spacing or assignment altered efficiency by less than 1 percentage point.
infographic.watch_item: Results are tied to a specific material stack, fixed thickness, and visible-band setting, so broader performance may differ under other fabrication tolerances or optical constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling Limits of Multichannel Spectral Routers for Snapshot Imaging

title: Continual-RL for Generalization in Autonomous Racing on the RoboRacer Platform
authors: Joel Siegert, Edoardo Ghignone, Michele Magno
abstract: A key challenge in modern robotics is to adapt to changing environments, a challenge that is exacerbated when simulations cannot encompass every possible real-world configuration, and therefore Reinforcement Learning (RL) in the physical world becomes necessary. Continual Reinforcement Learning provides the tools to address this challenge; however, both the frameworks and the methods remain underexplored. Autonomous Racing and in particular the RoboRacer competition provide a testing ground for such methods, as learning to drive on a new track-floor combination with the least amount of new experience naturally frames a continual learning problem. This work tries to address this gap by proposing a continual RL framework based on Continual Backpropagation that is able, with only real-world data, to train a generalistic policy on a set of tracks and then fine- tune it within 15 minutes to outperform classical controllers. Furthermore, a comparison method based on offline RL is proposed, and a simulation analysis of the plasticity properties of the methods is conducted.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that continual reinforcement learning can adapt a racing policy to new real-world track-floor combinations with minimal new experience, improving generalization and fast fine-tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For autonomous racing robotics, this offers a practical route to deploy controllers that keep learning on hardware where simulation cannot cover every environment variation.
method: Build a continual RL framework based on Continual Backpropagation.
Train a generalistic policy directly from real-world data across multiple tracks.
Fine-tune the policy in about 15 minutes and compare against classical controllers and an offline RL baseline.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports real-world training on a set of tracks, 15-minute fine-tuning, and a simulation analysis of plasticity, with the goal of outperforming classical controllers.
infographic.watch_item: Results may depend on the specific RoboRacer hardware, track-floor conditions, and the stability/plasticity tradeoff of continual backpropagation, so transferability to other platforms is not guaranteed.
infographic.paper_title: Continual-RL for Generalization in Autonomous Racing on the RoboRacer Platform
